q1: I cooked beans after school with firewood. The pot took long and smoke entered the room while my younger brother was doing homework.
q2: I first heard about pressure cookers from a youth savings group. I liked faster beans but worried about the sound and price.
q3: My aunt says the cooker saves charcoal, but a neighbor says it can burst if young people use it carelessly.
q4: The hard part is convincing my mother that I can use it safely and that savings should go to a device we have not tried.
q5: If it worked, evening cooking would finish earlier and I could study without waiting for beans to soften.

current_cooking_methods: charcoal stove; purchased meals on busy days
q1: My wife cooked rice and sauce on charcoal. The charcoal was damp and she had to fan it many times.
q2: I heard about pressure cookers at a market demonstration near Muhoza. The vendor cooked beans quickly and explained the safety valve.
q3: Other riders said it is useful if the seller can show where spare seals are found. They trust demonstrations more than radio talk.
q4: We considered buying one, but we need a clear warranty and someone local who can explain maintenance.
q5: We may spend less on charcoal and my wife could prepare food before evening customers call me.

q1: I cooked cassava leaves with firewood collected by my daughter. Rain made the wood wet and smoke made my eyes water.
q2: I heard about pressure cookers from a health worker during a nutrition visit. It sounded modern but far from our village shop.
q3: Women in our group say clean cooking helps children, but some say replacement parts are only in town.
q4: The decision is difficult because the health message is convincing but the purchase and repair path is unclear.
q5: If training and spare parts were near us, I would use less firewood and keep smoke away from children.

q1: I cooked beans before going to the market. With charcoal I had to start very early and check the pot while preparing goods.
q2: I heard about pressure cookers from a customer who uses one with LPG. I feared pressure until she showed me the locking lid.
q3: In the market some women say fast cooking helps business days. Others wait to see who has used it for months.
q4: The difficult part was safety fear, but a demonstration and written instructions reduced that fear.
q5: I can cook before opening the stall and avoid buying lunch outside.

q1: We cooked maize and beans for a meeting using firewood behind the cooperative office. Younger members complained about smoke.
q2: I heard about pressure cookers in a district agriculture meeting. I respected the time saving but wondered whether food would taste familiar.
q3: People ask leaders to try first. If respected households approve the taste, others will follow.
q4: The difficult part is not only money. It is changing a cooking habit that signals hospitality during meetings.
q5: If leaders test it publicly, clean cooking could become a sign of organized and modern households.

q4: I want one but the first cost competes with school fees and rent.
q5: With a payment plan, I would bring work skills home and spend less time cooking after work.

q1: I cooked sweet potatoes using firewood. I know smoke is bad, but I understand this stove and control the fire.
q2: I heard about pressure cookers from a radio program but did not see one closely. The word pressure made me afraid.
q3: Young people say it is safe, but older women say instructions are hard to remember.
q4: I want less smoke but fear making a mistake with a sealed pot.
q5: If someone trained me slowly in Kinyarwanda and checked my first uses, I might consider it.

q4: The hard part is knowing which model is reliable and not buying a fake product.
q5: With trusted vendor lists, I would support buying one and show friends how it works.
